stages.name: Public expenditure and its effects
stages.title: Public expenditure and its effects
stages.sub: How the size of government spending relative to GDP affects living standards, taxes, equality, and how we then measure poverty and inequality.

steps.q: A government raises spending on hospitals and schools from 20% of GDP to 35% of GDP. Are citizens likely to have better healthcare and education as a result?
steps.right: Yes, access to these services improves
steps.wrong: No, GDP itself must rise first
steps.hint: Think about what the extra money is actually spent on.

steps.q: That extra hospital and school spending has to be paid for somehow. Where does the government's money mostly come from?
steps.right: Taxes it collects from people and firms
steps.wrong: Extra output the private sector produces for free
steps.hint: Government cannot spend what it hasn't first collected or borrowed.

steps.q: Two households both earn £30,000 a year. One has £29,000 left after paying rent, bills and food. The other has only £1,000 left. Do they have the same standard of living, even though their incomes are equal?
steps.right: No, the second is much worse off
steps.wrong: Yes, since their incomes are identical
steps.hint: Equal income does not always mean equal ability to afford basic needs.

steps.q: To compare countries or track progress over time, would economists rather just say 'some people are poor and unequal', or use an agreed measure like the share of income going to the poorest 10%, or an income line below which someone counts as poor?
steps.wrong: A vague description is just as useful
steps.hint: Think about what is needed to compare years or countries consistently.
